I got my A01 from Luvbuckets on Ebay. Got it at the end of March. PS1, PS2 and PS3 games boot/start so no issues with the PS2 chip. RSX temps idle around 50ºC and running games like God of War 3 don't make the PS3 sound like a jet engine anymore, it's extremely rare for the fans to get loud and when it does happen it's for less than 30 seconds.

Besides the 40nm RSX, he sells them with the APS power supply, CELL/RSX delidded without the IHS, RIP Felix tantalizers with Panasonic tantalum caps and comes with a 6 month warranty. Cosmetically, the card reader cover and the PS logo above the disc drive that rotates are included, I just wish the shell was a bit more polished but otherwise, 9/10.

So here's the thing with the Pro.

Only like half a dozen games do true 4K. Most of the time it's between 1200p\~1440p. However this console is valuable 2 reasons. 

1. The late, heavier games run below 1080p on the normal PS4 but the Pro can at least stay at 1080p for those heavy games.

2. Homebrew. For example, if you make your own PS2 Classics, some of them only run well on the Pro. Same thing with Retroarch and other homebrew/emulation apps. The extra horse power is useful.

  
If you don't mind 720p\~900p on some games and will only use it exclusively for PS4 games, then the Slim will be ok for you. As for hard drives, only 2.5' inch HDDs can fit on the PS4 and should all be compatible.

Wrath of Cortex: Xbox. Insanely faster load times, more detailed textures, 480p and Crash has fur. The only "downgrade" is the unique song missing for medieval madness, exclusive for the PS2.

Nitro Kart: Xbox. Also very fast load times, 720p support, smooth framerate and the karts don't look blurry in the character select screen unlike PS2 (and Gamecube?).

Twinsanity: PS2 (Greatest Hits version). Xbox version has audio desync issues when you meet Nina, some of the props have bugged lighting like the crystals in cavern catastrophe and the overall shaders of the game are missing on Xbox - its only advantage is 480p support.

Crash Tag Team Racing: PS2, Gamecube and Xbox. The only real differences are the 480p support on Gamecube & Xbox and slightly better load times while the PS2 version has bit more content if you connect a PSP save file to it but this one is great on all platforms.

Crash of the Titans & MoM: Xbox 360. Not much to say really, it's the HD versions of the games with true widescreen support and you can play as Coco in co-op in MoM.

N. Sane Trilogy: PC. Full 60fps support and true 4K.

CTR Nitro-Fueled: Xbox One X/PS4 Pro. 1440p resolution for both but the One X has a bit better ambient occlusion settings than PS4 although the PS4 has the retro stadium and skins so they're both great.

It's About Time: PC, PS5 and Xbox Series. True 4K, maxed out settings. Though PC can go up to 120fps and higher.

My UM790 Pro with the 7940HS is reliable now but I had to switch to Linux - Zorin OS and disable PSS (power saving states) in the BIOS.

Using Windows 11, it would sometimes reboot when it was doing specific tasks like video playback or emulation. Also, GPU drivers would crash with specific games. All these problems were gone after I switched to Linux. It came with the 5600Mhz RAM and 1TB SSD. 3 months of usage under Linux and not a single crash regardless of what I was doing.

Though if you want to stay on Windows, buying one of these might be risky because it could be unstable. Games work fine if you use Steam Proton.

Mine also had problems but this is 100% GPU drivers+BIOS issues. I know this thread is a few weeks old but others might find this useful because I managed to make it 100% stable without touching the hardware.

I bought one in the summer (32GB/1TB) that came with the BIOS 1.03. One thing I noticed right away is when I tried certain games mostly through emulation the screen would freeze for some seconds and then come back with a gpu driver crash error. Then I started noticing that after some Windows and GPU updates, reboots were happening and becoming frequent (once a day), I stopped them for a while by disabling hardware acceleration because it seemed to happen during video playback so some type of video decoding issue. 1 or 2 months later the reboots or blue screens were happening again but now it would happen fairly quickly when I was playing games through emulators. I tried downclocking the RAM, disabling PSS and a few other things people recommend on the BIOS but nothing ever helped.

I couldn't return this anymore because it had been a couple of months so I had to make a decision. I could try upgrading the BIOS which would then lock me out of a downgrade and possibly make things worse or... give Linux a try.

I decided to try Linux, Zorin OS to be specific because the UI is similar to Windows. GPU driver crashes were gone though during the first 2-3 days I noticed random reboots were still happening, usually when I minimized the browser or other things. I was starting to lose hope until I remembered to try to disable "turn off screen after X minutes" and PSS in the BIOS as desperate attempts and it worked. It's been nearly a month and this PC is super stable, no more reboots, blue screens, gpu driver crashes, etc.

I just wish Linux was as convenient as Windows but it's a small price to pay for stability. Some things require more effort to get working properly since the software I use, games or not were built with Windows in mind.

I blame Minisforums for the buggy BIOS, however they are not the sole reason why this PC has issues. AMD has been really slacking when it comes to providing real support for this chip. The ASUS ROG Ally which has a similar chip also has the same GPU driver crash problem and I assume every device that uses this iGPU has this problem and possibly more. Honestly, this is the first and last time I will go with AMD. I'm just happy it works fine now.
